newsitem.title: USA: Lockheed sees strong fight with Boeing for jets.
newsitem.headline: Lockheed sees strong fight with Boeing for jets.

text.p: A Lockheed Martin Corp. official said on Saturday he expects rival Boeing Co. to be a strong competitor in the race to win a contract to build 3,000 new generation fighter jets.

"They very badly want to win," Micky Blackwell, president and chief operating officer of the aeronautics sector at Lockheed, said at a news conference at the National Press Club. "We're going to have our hands full."

The Pentagon announced it had selected Lockheed and Boeing to compete for the contract to build a "joint strike fighter," a jet for use by several branches of the U.S. armed forces and the British Royal Navy. A third team led by McDonnell Douglas Corp. was eliminated from the running.
The Defense Department said it was awarding Lockheed a $718.8 million contract and Boeing a $661.8 million contract to immediately begin work on their prototypes.

Blackwell rejected a suggestion that Boeing could not compete against Lockheed, the nation's biggest defense contractor, and said making today's cut was only just the beginning. "We've been in the end zone many times, but the game is not won," he said.

Blackwell said that Lockheed's experience working with Boeing, a subcontractor on Lockheed's F22 fighter program, has shown that the company will be a formidable competitor. While Boeing is the world's biggest builder of commercial jets, it has not built a fighter jet since World War II, and was considered the underdog in the competition by many.
Lockheed Martin expects to get into a "bidding war" with Boeing to get British Aerospace Plc on board, Blackwell said. British Aerospace was previously part of the McDonnell Douglas team.

"I think BAE is in a positiion to be a significant part of this program," Blackwell said. He also said that they would consider working with McDonnell Douglas and other U.S. and British companies to produce its fighter prototype. Blackwell said that he expected that the Joint Strike Fighter program will be worth up to $500 billion, much more than the $170 billion predicted by analysts. In addition to 3,000 joint strike fighters now planned for the U.S. Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps and the British Royal Navy, industry executives believe another 1,000 could be sold for export to U.S. allies, where Blackwell said the winner could bring in additional revenue.

Lockheed Martin will increase its work force to create a prototype for the project, but not significantly, as it currently has a large group of engineers and managers it can draw upon. "I don't think that you will see any ground swell in hiring," Blackwell said.
Blackwell predicted that the company will hire 400 people for its Ft. Worth, Texas, operations, and 700 people in its Palmdale, Calif., plant.

The radar-avoiding "stealth" jet is the biggest arms project of the early 21st century and would provide a common attack jet with variations for the United States and Great Britain. Lockheed and Boeing will now build competing test models for a final selection in the year 2001. The first jets are scheduled for delivery in 2008.
